In [[mathematics]], the '''Paley–Wiener integral''' is a simple [[stochastic integral]]. When applied to [[Abstract Wiener space|classical Wiener space]], it is less general than the [[Itô integral]], but the two agree when they are both defined.

The integral is named after its discoverers, [[Raymond Paley]] and [[Norbert Wiener]].

==Definition==
Let <math>i : H \to E</math> be an [[abstract Wiener space]] with abstract Wiener measure <math>\gamma</math> on <math>E</math>. Let <math>j : E^* \to H</math> be the [[adjoint of an operator|adjoint]] of <math>i</math>. (We have abused notation slightly: strictly speaking, <math>j : E^* \to H^*</math>, but since <math>H</math> is a [[Hilbert space]], it is [[Isometry|isometrically isomorphic]] to its [[dual space]] <math>H^*</math>, by the [[Riesz representation theorem]].)

It can be shown that <math>j</math> is an [[injective function]] and has [[dense (topology)|dense]] [[image (function)|image]] in <math>H</math>.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} Furthermore, it can be shown that every [[linear functional]] <math>f \in E^*</math> is also [[square-integrable]]: in fact,

:<math>\| f \|_{L^{2} (E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})} = \| j(f) \|_{H}</math>

This defines a natural [[linear map]] from <math>j(E^*)</math> to <math>L^2(E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})</math>, under which <math>j(f) \in j(E^*) \subseteq H</math> goes to the [[equivalence class]] <math>[f]</math> of <math>f</math> in <math>L^2(E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})</math>. This is well-defined since <math>j</math> is injective. This map is an [[isometry]], so it is [[continuous function|continuous]].

However, since a continuous linear map between [[Banach space]]s such as <math>H</math> and <math>L^2(E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})</math> is uniquely determined by its values on any dense subspace of its domain, there is a unique continuous linear extension <math>I : H \to L^2(E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})</math> of the above natural map <math>j(E^*) \to L^2(E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})</math> to the whole of <math>H</math>.

This isometry <math>I : H \to L^2(E, \gamma; \mathbb{R})</math> is known as the '''Paley–Wiener map'''. <math>I(h)</math>, also denoted <math>\langle h, x \rangle^\sim</math>, is a function on <math>E</math> and is known as the '''Paley–Wiener integral''' (with respect to <math>h \in H</math>).

The Paley–Wiener integral for a particular element <math>h \in H</math> is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] on <math>E</math>. The notation <math>\langle h, x \rangle^\sim</math> does not really denote an inner product (since <math>h</math> and <math>x</math> belong to two different spaces), but is a convenient [[abuse of notation]] in view of the [[Cameron–Martin theorem]]. For this reason, many authors{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} prefer to write <math>\langle h, - \rangle^\sim (x)</math> or <math>I(h)(x)</math> rather than using the more compact but potentially confusing <math>\langle h, x \rangle^\sim</math> notation.
